newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker leery on rushing US stock decimalization.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker leery on rushing US stock decimalization.

text.p: Rep. Scott Klug said Monday he is concerned about Congress moving quickly on a bill that would move stock quoting in the United States to dollars and cents from fractions.

"It's not that I'm opposed; I don't think there is any hurry to do this. It's worked for 300 years and it seems to me if it takes another three months or three years it won't be the end of the world," the Wisconsin Republican told reporters at the North American Securities Administrators Association's conference here.

Klug is a member of the House Commerce Committee's subcommittee on Finance, which is considering a measure that would mandate the nation's stock exchanges to eventually trade stocks in decimals rather than in fractions.

Such a shift would enable investors to save money in transactions costs because there would be a narrow difference between the prices at which they buy and sell stocks, supporters of the legislation say.

Others, including the subcommittee's ranking minority member Thomas Manton, a New York Democrat, have echoed the concerns raised by securities industry officials, warning that such a move could be disruptive and is a decision to be made by the markets rather than by Congress.

Nonetheless, Klug noted the decimalization measure is the first major issue on the House panel's radar screen, but he warned more study is needed. "It seems to me that we need to be careful when we do this," the lawmaker told state securities regulators attending the conference. "Often times the law of unintended consequences takes place."
Klug questioned whether such a move would have a bad impact on small companies with thinly-traded stocks.

"As somebody who represents Madison, Wisconsin, where we have a lot of hi-tech companies and a lot of bio-tech companies, that is a real interesting question," he said. "I'm not sure AT&T (Corp), Honeywell (Inc) and 3M (Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co) are really going to be affected by this, but I worry about the small guys who want to become public, whether the markets will still exist."
